readerContract.humanQuestion: What does RubyGems confirm about the May package-spam incident, and what remains an attribution claim?

readerContract.centralMentalModel: A service can directly confirm activity and its response on its own system while lacking enough evidence to identify who authored or operated the code.
readerContract.dailyLifeConnection: A reader can assess any AI-linked incident headline by asking what the reporting organization observed itself and what it only attributes to someone else.
readerContract.surfaceJob: A short dated cybersecurity news explanation about incident evidence and attribution boundaries.
readerContract.desiredFeeling: I can take a security incident seriously without upgrading an unresolved attribution into a fact.

draftArchitecture.plainAnswer: RubyGems confirms a May package-spam campaign and its response, but not that AI agents created or published the packages.
causalSequence: RubyGems removed accounts and more than 500 packages, then investigated the activity.
The registry can report its direct observations but cannot determine AI authorship from its available evidence.
draftArchitecture.workedCase: A building manager can confirm that an unauthorized flyer was posted and removed, but not who designed it without evidence about the maker.
draftArchitecture.transferCase: For a new AI-linked incident, name the source that observed the event, the evidence it had, and whether responsibility is confirmed or attributed.
draftArchitecture.usefulAction: Before sharing an AI-incident claim, look for the organization’s direct statement and identify which sentence is observation versus attribution.
draftArchitecture.formatSpecificStructure: The Story; LAiDIES Read; What This Means for You; Cocktail Party; Class Notes.
draftArchitecture.antiTemplateDecision: Lead with the confirmed registry incident and use the attribution distinction as the mechanism; avoid operational package details and generic AI panic.
